profiles.heading: A device reporting every five minutes
profiles.subhead: What one device costs for one month, on the cheapest tier that legitimately fits the fleet. Every figure carries the date we last checked it against the vendor's own page.

rows.note: Perch is free to ten devices, Scale covers a thousand, Fleet covers ten thousand. The rate falls because the tier above is cheaper per device, not because anyone negotiated a discount.

A flat $0.25 for every device that connects, plus data, which is why the rate never moves with the fleet. That beats us up to roughly 1,225 devices and loses above it, so below that line we would rather you weighed the dashboard, organizations and alerting they do not ship than the price.

Free to five devices, $749 for a thousand on Business, and at ten thousand it is Private Cloud Launch at $1,499 plus five thousand extra devices at $0.10. Their meter counts data points rather than messages, so a device sending several readings per report reaches the ceiling long before its device count suggests.

Their overage rate does not fall between Pilot and Production, so a buyer minimizing cost would stay on Pilot at any size: $20,209 against $21,219 at ten thousand devices. Production buys an SLA, not a volume discount. Their free device count read inconsistently across two fetches, ten in the headline copy against thirty on the plan card, so treat that one as unconfirmed.

In fairness to them, Memfault is crash and firmware observability, not a telemetry platform, so this row is a scale reference rather than a like-for-like rival. Growth is $3,495 and Scale $6,695, and both include exactly a thousand monthly active devices with no overage rate published anywhere, which is why ten thousand has no figure at all. Their session cap is 15 per device per day on Growth and 25 on Scale, against this profile's 288, so the published pricing does not look designed for continuous telemetry. Their free tier is limited to Nordic parts.

Sold in whole $299 blocks of 100 devices and 720,000 data operations; a thousand devices needs thirteen of them and ten thousand needs 122. There is no per-operation overage rate at all, so one operation over the line buys another entire block.

$0.00075 per event that arrives, flat, whatever its size, which is why the rate is almost identical at every fleet size. Frequent small reports are the worst case for that model. Cellular data rides with the Notecard hardware and is not counted here.

Starter at $49 includes a million inputs a month and Scale at $199 is written as a million and up, without saying up to what. This profile crosses a million inputs at about 114 devices, and their page publishes no overage rate at all, which is what makes both larger fleets genuinely unpriceable rather than merely expensive. There is a free plan for five devices, but its input allowance is not published either, so the single-device column prices Starter.

Their pricing page answered HTTP 429 on six attempts across several URLs, and again on a later re-check, so this is how their site behaves rather than one bad afternoon. The aggregator figures that turn up in search are unverified. We would rather leave this row empty than publish a number we cannot stand behind.

build_your_own.note: Costed line by line at this profile rather than taken from a headline rate: messaging, connectivity, shadow operations, the rules engine, Jobs for the firmware update, and the time-series writes. Those writes are DynamoDB, they are 59% of the total, and they never appear on the IoT pricing page at all.
The same build with each report's four readings written as one item, which is what a competent team would do. We quote this one too rather than only the figure that flatters us.

The cheapest raw number in this whole comparison, and the one a technical buyer is most likely to have anchored on. Azure's pricing page renders its figures in the browser and returns nothing to a plain fetch, so these came from the public Retail Prices API for us-east.
The same hub once firmware updates are added, at $70 a month per instance plus $0.07 per device. This is the honest comparison of the two, because shipping devices you cannot update is not a product.

profiles.heading: The same device, reporting every ten seconds
profiles.subhead: Nothing changes but the cadence. This is where metering models stop agreeing with each other, and where a buyer finds out which unit their vendor really charges in.

rows.note: One device at this cadence fits inside Perch's 300,000 message pool, though it then starves the account's other nine. At a thousand devices it is $0.35 of base plus $6.45 of overage. We are not the cheapest here and are not going to pretend otherwise.

The clearest win for a per-device rate that barely moves with traffic. At this cadence they beat us outright, and the answer we would give you is the dashboard, organizations and alerting rather than the number.

At five readings per report a single device emits 1.3 million data points a month against the free tier's one million ceiling, while using barely half its message allowance. That is a cliff at one device, on a limit nobody was watching. At a thousand the same arithmetic forces the jump to Private Cloud even though the device count fits Business exactly.
One chatty device exhausts a whole $299 block of data operations by itself, and blocks are the only unit on offer.
A flat charge per event, whatever its size, meets a device that sends 259,200 tiny events a month.

profiles.closing: Blues at $194 per device per month for a ten-second cadence is the clearest illustration of why a flat charge per event is the wrong model for small frequent reports, and it is the clearest opening we have.

build_your_own.note: Time-series writes are 73% of it at this cadence, up from 59% at five minutes. The cost of a chatty device on AWS is almost entirely the cost of storing what it says.
